**17 records.** \[[Davies 2020][research_davies_2020]\] \[[Davies 2025][research_davies_2025]\] \[[Harris 1989][research_harrisjr_1989]\] \[[History of Supersonic Transport 2020][research_history_of_2020]\] \[[Volkov 2023][research_hypersonic_and_2023]\] \[[James 1998][research_james_1998]\] \[[Nadim Melhem et al. 2024][research_nadimmelhem_richardmunroe_2024]\] \[[Petrescu 2020][research_petrescu_2020]\] \[[Seebass 1997][research_seebass_1997]\] \[[Spearman 1979][research_spearman_1979]\] \[[Supersonic and Hypersonic Flight 1960][research_supersonic_and_1960]\] \[[SUPERSONIC FLIGHT 2014][research_supersonic_flight_2014]\] \[[Supersonic Flight 2025][research_supersonic_flight_2025]\] \[[Transonic and Supersonic Flight 1992][research_transonic_and_1992]\] \[[Trimpi 1980][research_trimpi_1980]\] \[[Wegener 1991][research_wegener_1991]\] \[[Wegener 1997][research_wegener_1997]\]

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**The familiar framing is that the X-59 is a quiet supersonic aeroplane built to show that a quiet boom can satisfy the rule, and the framing breaks down in five places.**

**There is no loudness in the rule to satisfy.** The prohibition bans a speed and the exemption path requires the absence of a measurable boom, so a quiet boom meets neither, as argued under The Rule It Exists to Change Contains No Loudness at All \[[14 CFR 91.817][ref_far_91_817]\] \[[14 CFR 91.818][ref_far_91_818]\].

**The ninety percent that has been published is not a loudness.** The nearest ratio to it is a ratio of overpressures, while in perceived loudness the reduction is 47.8 percent against the commonly quoted baseline, a calculation given in Where the Ninety Percent Comes From.

**The quiet is not wholly the aeroplane's to deliver.** Loudness is set by rise time and rise time is set by the atmosphere, and the equivalent area the weight contributes cannot be shaped away, as the parts headed What Classical Theory Says the Rise Time Should Be and The Weight Puts an Equivalent Area There and No Shaping Removes It argue.

**A quiet boom is not the only answer to a boom over land.** Cruise below the cutoff Mach number makes no ground boom at all, and the X-59 flies above it on purpose because its question needs a boom to exist, as recorded in The Aeroplane Could Have Avoided the Problem Entirely and Refuses To.

**And the framing speaks in the present tense about an aeroplane that had not yet made a boom.** The register wrote its claim in the future tense, and at the date of this article the future tense was still correct.

## The Source Base

**72 hand-written references carry the argument and 2,572 research records map the field, and this article keeps them apart on purpose.** The claims about what a document does and does not contain rest on five documents read in full, being the register, the two sections of the federal aviation regulations, the executive order directing their repeal, and the programme's own conference presentation. **Those are not commentary on the evidence. They are the evidence.**

### The Research References

**The survey holds 2,572 research records drawn from NASA's Technical Reports Server, the Defense Technical Information Center and the journal literature**, of which 480 are report primaries, being 18.7 percent, by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary. **The median publication year is 2006.** Of the 2,442 dated records, 324 were published before 1973, the year the prohibition on civil supersonic flight over the United States took effect, being 13.3 percent, and 683 were published in 2018 or later, the year this aeroplane was designated, being 28.0 percent \[[Civil Aircraft Sonic Boom, final rule][ref_fr_1973_sonic_boom]\].

**This programme publishes no index of its own reports.** The project page for the agency's commercial supersonic work carries an editor's note saying the project has concluded and is no longer updated, and it links to no publications list at all \[[Commercial Supersonic Technology Project][ref_nasa_cst]\].

**Each record sits in one cluster, chosen by reading its title.** The literature that treats the sonic boom or supersonic flight as a whole has clusters of its own, so no cluster is a residual.

### The Word the Programme Uses Is Not the Word the Field Uses

**The programme says sonic thump and the literature says sonic boom.** Counting each of the 2,572 research titles once and ignoring case, 5 contain the phrase sonic thump and 906 contain the phrase sonic boom. **A programme's chosen word is a communications decision and the literature keeps its own**, so the article uses the field's word except where it is quoting.

### Five Governing Documents Were Read in Full and Counted

**The regulatory half of this article rests on 5 documents totalling 206,232 characters, every one retrieved and read.** They are the two sections of the regulation, the 2021 final rule that put them in their present form, the 2020 proposal to bring supersonic aeroplanes into the noise certification rules, and the one authorisation to exceed Mach 1 that has been granted and noticed.

**The phrase sonic boom appears 62 times across them and the programme's own metric appears 0.** **A claim that a document does not say something is a count of zero, and a count of zero is the easiest kind of claim to get wrong**, so it is computed from the retrieved text. The aeroplane itself is named 0 times, against 16 mentions of the agency that operates it.

**A preamble is a primary document about what an agency decided and why**, and it is the only place the reasoning behind a regulation is written down. Reading the rulemaking as well as the regulation is the difference between knowing what a rule says and knowing what its author thinks it means.

### Where the Displayed Relations Come From

**The article displays 60 relations and evaluates all but 3 of them**, and those 3 are named in the epistemic state as boundaries rather than presented as results.

**Lockheed Martin publishes a product card carrying the gross weight, the empty weight, the fuel, the payload, an overall length and a design Mach number.** Every weight this article uses comes from it, including those in the lift-induced equivalent area and in the range relation, whose unknowns reduce to one.

**The boom carpet is computed by tracing rays through the standard atmosphere from the Mach cone to the ground**, using the invariance of the horizontal slowness. Run at Mach 2, the same trace agrees with the literature's rule of thumb of a statute mile of carpet per thousand feet of altitude to within 3.9 percent, and that agreement is the evidence for the Mach 1.4 answer.

### The Regulatory Text Is Quoted From Saved Copies

**The electronic Code of Federal Regulations answers an automated request with about ten kilobytes of navigation for a section that is eighty kilobytes in a browser, and the clause this article quotes is not in the ten.** Both sections are therefore quoted from copies retrieved with a browser and saved. The Federal Register site redirects an automated request to an unblock page, so the executive order is read from a university archive of the same text, and both addresses are cited.

### One Catalogue Record Misspells Its Own Title

**The library index records Maglieri's 2014 survey of the field as `Soinc boom`.** The reference list gives the title the work actually has, and a reader following the link will see the misspelling in the catalogue record.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is on NASA's Technical Reports Server or it carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. **The report-primary fraction is 18.7 percent, being 480 of the 2,572 research records.** The rule does not reach the journal papers among the sources this article's derivations use, such as Whitham on the flow pattern of a supersonic projectile, Stevens on the Mark VII perceived level and Pierce on rise times, so 18.7 percent is a lower bound on how much of the survey is first-hand.

### Thin Subjects

**Seven subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, case ignored and a hyphen read as a space.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---:|
| the ground reflection factor and the impedance of the ground | reflection factor, reflection factors, ground impedance, impedance of the ground | 2 |
| the structure and thickness of a weak shock | shock structure, shock wave structure, shock thickness, shock wave thickness | 2 |
| the perceived level as a metric | perceived level, Mark VII, PLdB | 6 |
| Concorde as the baseline | Concorde | 4 |
| the weight of the aeroplane in its signature | weight | 1 |
| skin friction at supersonic speed | skin friction | 1 |
| the range relation and the fuel consumption | Breguet, fuel consumption | 7 |

**The ground reflection factor rests on 2 titles.** One gives reflection factors for flight near the threshold Mach number and the other estimates the impedance of the ground from a microphone array, so the impedance of 19 that the conventional factor of 1.9 implies is this article's own reading and not a measured value.

**The classical shock thickness is named in 2 titles**, one of which concludes that molecular relaxation is insufficient to explain the shock structure of sonic booms. The Taylor thickness this article computes comes from the textbook relation it displays.

**The perceived level is named in 6 titles**, one of them Stevens's definition of the Mark VII scale and the rest its application to sonic booms. **Concorde is named in 4 titles and none of them names a perceived level**, so the survey does not settle the baseline against which the programme's reduction is stated.

**The weight of an aeroplane is named in 1 title**, a study of overpressure trends with weight, altitude, Mach number and shaping, so the reading that this aeroplane's weight rather than its shape dominates its equivalent area rests on the relation shown and not on a body of measurement.

**Skin friction is named in 1 title**, on supersonic and hypersonic skin friction with transition, so the friction coefficient this article computes rests on the flat-plate relation it displays. **The range relation is named in 7 titles and 1 of them concerns a supersonic aeroplane**, a 1965 study of cruise fuel consumption and track selection in supersonic transport operations.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on a subject this article's argument uses.** Those subjects are the aeroplane and its predecessors, the generation, prediction, propagation and measurement of the boom, its effects on buildings, animals and people, the rule and the certification of aircraft noise, the supersonic aerodynamics, propulsion, vision system and cruise performance the sizing reasons with, and the atmosphere the boom crosses.

**The records excluded are those whose only link to the article is a shared word or a distant application.** Overpressure is also the measure of an explosive blast, and the literature of blast injury to the brain, the lungs, the eyes and the ears is large. Impulsive noise is also an outlier in a communications channel, atmospheric turbulence also distorts a laser beam, and a caustic is also made of light. Sonic hedgehog is one of the most cited genes in developmental biology. An economic boom, a baby boom, a crane boom, a refuelling boom and an oil containment boom are all boom, and a gene expression signature, a digital signature, a radar signature and a mutational signature are all signature. Breguet is also a family of watchmakers, and QUESST is also the abbreviation of a 2014 speech retrieval benchmark. Supersonic is also the flow in a scramjet combustor, around a projectile or a missile and through an ejector, and shock focusing is also a technique of medicine and of detonation research, and those records are excluded. The noise of roads, railways, wind turbines and machines shares the psychoacoustics of a boom and none of its source, and the handling qualities of aeroplanes in general share the cockpit and not the missing window, so they are excluded too. **Correction, erratum and withdrawal notices are excluded because they are not research works.** Reviews of books, reference and definition entries, other notices such as news items and editorials, and a second deposit of a document already in the survey are excluded for the same reason.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept because they share this subject's science rather than only its words.** The long-range atmospheric propagation of weak blast waves and of infrasound, general nonlinear acoustics, the annoyance of military impulsive noise and of helicopters, the certification of the noise of subsonic aircraft, and the handling qualities of supersonic aeroplanes are the main examples, and a reader may weigh each accordingly.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only.

## Epistemic State

### Historical Fact

The X-59A designation was allocated on 21 June 2018 to Lockheed Martin with NASA as sponsor, and its mission statement in the register is the one quoted \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. NASA announced the design and build contract on 3 April 2018 at 247.5 million dollars, stating a period of performance ending 31 December 2021 and an intention to fly over selected United States cities beginning in mid-2022 \[[NASA Release 18-020][ref_nasa_release_18_020]\]. The aeroplane first flew on 28 October 2025 for 67 minutes, reaching approximately 12,000 feet and 230 miles per hour with the landing gear down, from Palmdale to Edwards \[[X-59 First Flight][ref_nasa_first_flight]\]. Lockheed Martin's product card gives a maximum design gross weight of 24,300 pounds, an empty weight of 15,000, fuel of 8,000, payload of 600, an overall length of 93.83 feet, a wingspan of 29 feet 6 inches, a design Mach number of 1.4, a loudness of less than 75 perceived level decibels and a single F414-GE-100 \[[Silencing the Sonic Boom, X-59 Product Card][ref_lm_card]\]. The design cruise condition is Mach 1.4 at 55,000 feet and the design target is 75 on the Stevens Mark VII perceived level scale \[[NASA Release 18-020][ref_nasa_release_18_020]\] \[[Doebler and Rathsam 2020][research_doebler_rathsam_2019]\]. Executive Order 14304 of 6 June 2025 directs the repeal of the prohibition within 180 days and the establishment of an interim noise-based certification standard, without naming a threshold \[[Executive Order 14304, American Presidency Project][ref_eo_14304_apps]\]. **The deadline fell on 3 December 2025 and the sections quoted in this article carry no amendment later than 15 January 2021** \[[14 CFR 91.817][ref_far_91_817]\] \[[14 CFR 91.818][ref_far_91_818]\]. The register's other sonic boom row, the X-54A, describes an aeroplane to be capable of generating relevant ground sonic boom signatures, so both rows describe an aeroplane that would make signatures and only the X-59A row calls its signature shaped. **The X-59A entry is half present tense and half future**, saying that the aircraft **is** a research aircraft and that it **will create** a shaped sonic boom signature.

### Recomputed From the Register by This Article

The register, in the copy the compiler last updated on 23 August 2026, carries 539 allocation rows of which 31 are X designations. **2 rows of the 539 mention a sonic boom and they are the X-54A and the X-59A.** **The word create appears in 1 row.** Measured without popular names and note markers, the X-59A mission statement is 84 characters against a median of 109 for the X rows and 328 for its immediate predecessor, placing it twenty-fourth of 31 by length. 94 rows have an empty engines cell. Lockheed Martin holds 6 X rows and NASA sponsors 10. **Every one of these is a count over the register file, and none is taken from a secondary source.** The copy counted here is later than this article's date, and the version current on that date carried 526 rows of which 29 were X designations, with the counts that differ under it stated in the opening section \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, 11 August 2025][ref_mds_addendum_2025]\].

### Verified by Reading the Document

**5 governing documents totalling 206,232 characters were retrieved and read in full**, being the two sections of the regulation, the 2021 final rule that put them in their present form, the 2020 proposal to bring supersonic aeroplanes into the noise certification rules, and the one authorisation to exceed Mach 1 that has been granted and noticed \[[14 CFR 91.817][ref_far_91_817]\] \[[14 CFR 91.818][ref_far_91_818]\] \[[Special Flight Authorizations for Supersonic Aircraft, final rule][ref_fr_2021_sfa]\] \[[Noise Certification of Supersonic Airplanes, proposed rule][ref_fr_2020_part36]\] \[[Petition for Authorization to Exceed Mach 1, notice of decision to grant][ref_fr_2024_boom]\]. Every passage quoted is quoted from what was read.

**Across all five, the phrase sonic boom appears 62 times and the programme's own metric appears 0.** The abbreviation is absent, and so are the words behind it. **The aeroplane is named 0 times**, against 16 mentions of the agency that operates it.

The design feature annotations attributed to NASA were read from the project's conference presentation \[[Richwine, X-59 Aircraft Overview and Status][ref_x59_overview]\], and the weights, the overall length and the loudness bound were read from the builder's product card \[[Silencing the Sonic Boom, X-59 Product Card][ref_lm_card]\].

### Analysis

The cutoff Mach number of 1.153 at the cruise altitude, and the finding that the cutoff ratio nowhere exceeds 1.153 in the standard atmosphere. The reproduction of the published 925 miles per hour to within 0.1 percent, and the identification of the released 940 miles per hour as Mach 1.42 at the same altitude. The conversion of 75 and 105 perceived level decibels to 2.134 and 4.088 sones and the resulting 47.8 percent. The classical Taylor rise time of 5.2 microseconds. The 19.9 decibel benefit of a tenfold rise time at 1,000 hertz. The slenderness ratios in the table.

The dynamic pressure of 12,512 pascals and the density of 0.14664 kilograms a cubic metre at the cruise condition. **The lift-induced equivalent area of 4.232 square metres and its growth by a factor of 2.06 between forty thousand feet and fifty-five.** The Reynolds number, the skin friction coefficient of 0.00206 and the friction drag of 25.7 newtons a square metre. The wave-drag ratio of 5.18 against a twenty metre body. **The boom carpet at 59.2 kilometres wide and the along-track offset of 19.29 kilometres, from a ray trace through the standard atmosphere that reproduces the literature's Mach 2 rule of thumb to within 3.9 percent.** The minimum signature duration of 73 milliseconds and the sound exposure level of 101 decibels. The classical absorption of 0.159 decibels a kilometre. The ground impedance of 19 that reproduces the conventional reflection factor.

The spread of 5.87 feet among the three published lengths and the shortfall of 700 pounds between the builder's weights and its stated total. The range of 47.8 to 53.1 percent across the published Concorde baselines, and the overpressure ratio of 84.5 percent. The equivalent diameter of 2.32 metres. The thrust bound of 2,634 pounds for an exponent of one. The first flight's 24.9 percent of the design cruise speed and 21.8 percent of the design cruise altitude.

All are computed from the published inputs named beside them by the relations displayed above, and every relation this article displays is evaluated except the three named below.

### Inference

**That the decomposition of the claimed 30 decibel reduction into 16.2 decibels of amplitude and 13.8 of shape is a bound rather than a measurement.** It assumes that perceived level would track peak overpressure by the decibel rule, which the preceding sections establish is false, and serves only to argue that shape cannot account for less than the residual.

**That the register's use of the verb create marks this row as different in kind.** The count of one is a fact. The reading that a shaped signature is a thing made rather than a phenomenon studied is this article's, and no one has been found stating it.

**That the aeroplane's configuration is dominated by cost and schedule wherever the boom does not constrain it.** The annotations are NASA's and the tally is this article's.

**That the aeroplane's weight rather than its shape is the majority contributor to its signature.** The relation is standard and the evaluation is arithmetic, but the reading is this article's, drawn from comparing a computed equivalent diameter of 2.32 metres against a fuselage whose slimness is visible rather than measured.

**That the aeroplane grew during detail design.** Three published lengths span 5.87 feet, the shortest is the builder's and carries a 2019 copyright while the longest are the agency's and are later. **No source states a growth and the alternative reading, that the figures measure to different points, is equally consistent.**

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**Whether the aeroplane will meet 75 perceived level decibels in flight.** By this article's date it had flown 1 time, subsonically, and no shaped signature had been produced or measured \[[X-59 First Flight][ref_nasa_first_flight]\] \[[NASA's X-59 Completes Second Flight][ref_nasa_second_flight]\].

**Whether the X-59 requires an authorisation under the rule.** The prohibition's text applies to a civil aircraft, the statute excludes public aircraft from civil aircraft, and no document read here applies that definition to this aeroplane or names it \[[49 U.S.C. 40102, Definitions][ref_usc_40102]\].

**The relative contribution of molecular relaxation and atmospheric turbulence to the observed rise time.** Both are documented, and the sources consulted do not agree on the split.

**Concorde's perceived level.** Published values include 105, 108 and 110 \[[NASA unveils a supersonic plane with a quiet boom, Physics Today][ref_feder_2024]\] \[[The Next NASA X-Plane, Born to Boom, Machine Design][ref_machinedesign_2018]\], and this article computes its headline comparison at 105, the value NASA's acousticians call commonly quoted, while giving the range the alternatives produce.

**The X-59's predicted ground overpressure.** The 0.3 pounds per square foot this article uses for illustration is the Quiet Supersonic Platform's shock goal \[[Iosifidis, Concept Development of the Quiet Supersonic Technology Aircraft][ref_iosifidis_2016]\], and the overpressure predicted for this aeroplane appears in none of the sources read.

**What form any replacement standard will take.** Executive Order 14304 requires an interim noise-based certification standard and does not say whether it would be written as a perceived level, an overpressure, or something else \[[Executive Order 14304, American Presidency Project][ref_eo_14304_apps]\], and at the editorial date no proposed rule had appeared \[[Federal Register search, FAA documents mentioning supersonic, 2016 to 4 December 2025][ref_fr_search_supersonic]\]. **A standard written as an overpressure would not use the metric in which this programme states its target**, and nothing read here settles which it will be.

**The lift-to-drag ratio and the thrust specific fuel consumption.** The builder's card supplies the weights, so the range relation has exactly one unknown, and that unknown is the ratio of the two. **The range and endurance given in the body are illustrative.**

**Whether the slenderness lowers the net drag.** Wave drag falls as the fourth power of length and wetted area rises as the first, which settles the direction of the trade but not its balance. **Whether the net drag falls depends on how the total divides between the two kinds at the design point, and no source publishes that division.**

**The wetted area and the volume of the equivalent body.** Without them the friction drag is given per square metre and never totalled, and the wave drag is given as a ratio against a shorter body and never evaluated absolutely.

**Why the builder's card does not add up.** The empty weight, the fuel and the payload sum to 700 pounds less than the gross weight the same card states \[[Silencing the Sonic Boom, X-59 Product Card][ref_lm_card]\], which is 2.9 percent, and no source explains the difference.

## Out of Scope

**The engineering of the eXternal Vision System beyond its existence and its validation.** It is a substantial subject in display design and human factors, outside aerodynamics.

**The economics of supersonic passenger transport.** Whether a market exists for a quieter supersonic airliner is a question about airlines and not about shock waves, and this article makes no claim either way.

**The environmental case beyond noise.** Fuel burn per passenger kilometre and stratospheric emissions are the other two objections to supersonic transport, both serious, and neither is what this aeroplane addresses.

**The rulemaking record before 1973 and the international one throughout.** The 1973 final rule and its appendix are read here only for their wording, and the proposals and hearings that preceded them are not examined. **The international standard-setting body's work on supersonic noise is a parallel process this article does not enter**, and the survey holds it without the argument using it.

**The commercial supersonic programmes.** One of them appears here only as a petitioner in the Federal Register and another only as a commenter on a rule. **Whether any of them will fly is not a question about this aeroplane**, and the trade press that follows them is not literature this survey admits.

**Every X-plane after the X-59.** The X-60A and beyond belong to later articles in this series.

## Conclusion

**The register gives this aeroplane one sentence and the sentence contains the whole programme in one adjective.** An aeroplane that will create a shaped sonic boom signature \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. The other of the register's two sonic boom rows, the [X-54][related_post_a351_gulfstream_x54], was to generate relevant ground signatures and was never built. **Both entries describe an aeroplane that would make signatures, and only one of them describes a shaped one.** That adjective is the difference between the two sentences, and the register's verb, used once in 539 rows, marks it. **One of the two was built.**

**The physics supports the ambition.** A signature that has not coalesced into a shock-fronted wave loses less energy on the way down and puts what remains at frequencies the ear discounts, and a factor of ten in rise time is worth 19.9 decibels at 1,000 hertz and twenty at every frequency well above both corners, which is where the ear does its listening. **The design problem is real, the mechanism is understood, and the aeroplane's extraordinary proportions are that mechanism made visible.**

**And the proportions may be cheaper than they look.** Wave drag falls as the fourth power of length and wetted area rises as the first, so the exponents favour length heavily. **Whether the net drag falls lies beyond this article**, because the answer depends on how the drag divides between the two kinds at the design point and no source publishes that division. What the exponents do establish is a direction. **Supersonic aeroplanes were long and thin before anybody cared what they sounded like**, so the shaping requirement pushed a shape the aerodynamics already wanted, **though it pushed it a good deal further**, this aeroplane being 1.39 times as slender as Concorde.

**What the shaping cannot touch is the weight.** Integrating the lift term of the equivalent area over the whole aeroplane leaves the weight divided by twice the dynamic pressure, with every trace of shape gone. At the design condition that is 4.232 square metres, a body 2.32 metres across, and **a designer may move it along the length and may not remove it**. Worse, it is inversely proportional to dynamic pressure, so **climbing to lengthen the propagation path enlarges it**, by a factor of 2.06 between forty thousand feet and the design altitude. **Two of the things altitude does to a sonic boom are therefore opposed**, and no source is cited for that reading, which is this article's inference. Altitude does others, changing the cutoff margin, the width of the carpet and the length of the absorbing path, and none of those is weighed here.

**Four things are less settled than the programme's public arithmetic suggests.**

**The claimed reduction is not ninety percent in any unit the target is stated in.** In perceived loudness it is 47.8 percent against the commonly quoted baseline, and between 47.8 and 53.1 percent across every baseline this article found. In pressure it is 96.8 percent and in energy 99.9. **The 84.5 percent that Concorde's overpressure against the low-boom goal gives is a pressure ratio, and reporting a pressure ratio as a loudness is the substitution this article warns against.** The Mark VII scale exists to prevent that substitution, and 30 decibels of perceived level is a little less than halving the loudness, because halving it takes 32.

**The baseline is part of the uncertainty and this article does not pretend otherwise.** Concorde's perceived level is published at 105, 108 and 110, the sources consulted do not agree, and the article computes its headline figure at 105 and shows what the alternatives give.

**The quantity that governs the answer is not under the designer's control.** Loudness is set by rise time, classical theory underestimates rise time by more than two orders of magnitude, and what makes up the difference is molecular relaxation and turbulence in the atmosphere on the day. **A predicted perceived level depends on the weather as much as on the aeroplane**, and the programme's plan is to fly over communities and survey the people underneath rather than to rely on computation \[[Quesst, NASA's mission to enable commercial supersonic flight][ref_nasa_quesst]\].

**And the rule the aeroplane exists to change contains no loudness at all.** The [X-54][related_post_a351_gulfstream_x54] established that it is a speed limit rather than a noise limit. This article read the rulemaking behind it and counted. **Across 5 governing documents and 206,232 characters, the programme's own metric appears 0 times.** The exemption path requires not a quiet boom but no measurable boom \[[14 CFR 91.818][ref_far_91_818]\]. The only noise standard ever proposed for supersonic aeroplanes governs them while they are flying subsonically, and it was never adopted \[[Noise Certification of Supersonic Airplanes, proposed rule][ref_fr_2020_part36]\] \[[Federal Register search, FAA documents mentioning supersonic, 2016 to 4 December 2025][ref_fr_search_supersonic]\]. **And on 15 January 2021, 2.6 years after this aeroplane was designated and while it was being built, the agency wrote down that the determination made in the 1970s that no level of sonic boom is acceptable over land still applies** \[[Special Flight Authorizations for Supersonic Aircraft, final rule][ref_fr_2021_sfa]\], against industry asking it to say otherwise.

**So the aeroplane's output is not compliance but evidence**, gathered so that a number might one day be written where none exists, and the executive order that would demand such a number declines to say what it should be.

**The deadline for writing it expired the day before this article.** The order of 6 June 2025 gave 180 days, the 3 December 2025 deadline came, and the regulation stood unchanged \[[Executive Order 14304, American Presidency Project][ref_eo_14304_apps]\] \[[14 CFR 91.817][ref_far_91_817]\]. **That is not a judgement about the programme or the agency**, since a rulemaking is slow and an executive deadline is not a statute. It is the state of the record at the date on this article.

**And what is being measured is not a point but a strip.** Tracing rays through the standard atmosphere, the carpet is 59.2 kilometres wide and the boom lands 19.29 kilometres behind the aeroplane that made it. **At Mach 2 the tracer agrees with the literature's rule of thumb to within 3.9 percent**, which is the reason to believe the Mach 1.4 figure, and the Mach 1.4 carpet is only 69.6 percent of the Mach 2 one. **Flying slower narrows the carpet as well as quietening it**, and the arithmetic gives that for nothing. **No source consulted for this article states it**, which describes what was read and is silent on what the programme says.

**At the editorial date the aeroplane had flown once, for 67 minutes, at 24.9 percent of its design cruise speed, with the landing gear down** \[[X-59 First Flight][ref_nasa_first_flight]\]. It had never been supersonic \[[NASA's X-59 Completes Second Flight][ref_nasa_second_flight]\]. The contract that built it named 31 December 2021 and the flights over cities were to begin in mid-2022 \[[NASA Release 18-020][ref_nasa_release_18_020]\]. **The register's claim about this aeroplane is written in the future tense, and at the time of writing the future tense was still correct.** The entry says that the aircraft **is** a research aircraft and that it **will create** a shaped sonic boom signature. The first half had been true since the aeroplane was rolled out. **The second half was still a promise.**

## Equations

<!-- Equations generated by _lib/equations.py from _sources/equations/. Edit the data file and regenerate. Do not edit this section by hand. -->

This section collects the 60 display equations of the article in the order they appear,
each under its number and reproduced exactly as it stands in the text.
A title in bold names an established result,
and a title in italics beginning with the word Bespoke names a construction made for this analysis.
Of the 60, 48 are established and 12 are bespoke.
Pressures, densities and speeds are in units of the International System at standard atmosphere conditions, while weights and thrusts are quoted from the builder in pounds and speeds from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration in miles per hour, levels are in decibels referred to 20 micropascals, and perceived level in decibels on the Mark VII scale is a psychophysical quantity whose differences are not pressure ratios, so a percentage reduction depends on whether it is stated in pressure, energy or loudness.

**Equation 1, Mach Angle and Prandtl-Glauert Parameter.**
The Mach cone has a half-angle whose sine is the reciprocal of the Mach number, and its cotangent is the Prandtl-Glauert parameter.
[Liepmann and Roshko, Elements of gasdynamics][book_liepmann]

$$
\sin\mu = \frac{1}{M}
\qquad\qquad
\cot\mu = \sqrt{M^2 - 1} = \beta
\tag{1}
$$

**Equation 2, Far-Field Overpressure From the F-Function.**
Linearised supersonic theory gives the far-field overpressure ratio as proportional to Whitham's F-function and inversely to the square root of distance.
[Whitham 1952][research_whitham_1952]
[Whitham, Linear and nonlinear waves][book_whitham]

$$
\frac{\Delta p}{p_a} = \frac{\gamma M^2}{\sqrt{2\beta r}}\; F(\zeta)
\tag{2}
$$

**Equation 3, Whitham F-Function.**
The F-function is an Abel transform of the second derivative of the equivalent area distribution.
[Whitham 1952][research_whitham_1952]
[Whitham, Linear and nonlinear waves][book_whitham]

$$
F(\zeta) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{\zeta}
\frac{A_e''(x)}{\sqrt{\zeta - x}}\; \mathrm{d}x
\tag{3}
$$

**Equation 4, Equivalent Area Including Lift.**
The equivalent area is the volume cross-section plus a term proportional to the lift carried ahead of each station.
[Ashley and Landahl, Aerodynamics of wings and bodies][book_ashley_landahl]
[Jones, Wing theory][book_jones]

$$
A_e(x) = A_V(x) + \frac{\beta}{2q} \int_0^{x} L'(\xi)\; \mathrm{d}\xi
\tag{4}
$$

**Equation 5, Lift-Induced Equivalent Area at the Tail.**
Integrated over the whole aircraft in level flight, the lift term collapses to the weight over twice the dynamic pressure times the Prandtl-Glauert parameter, independent of shape.

$$
A_e(\ell) - A_V(\ell) = \frac{\beta}{2q} \int_0^{\ell} L'(\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi
= \frac{\beta\,W}{2q}
\tag{5}
$$

*Equation 6, Bespoke Lift-Induced Equivalent Area at the Design Point.*
The equivalent area is evaluated with the published maximum design gross weight standing for the cruise lift, a choice the article makes, and the standard atmosphere dynamic pressure at Mach 1.4 and 55,000 feet.
[Silencing the Sonic Boom, X-59 Product Card][ref_lm_card]

$$
\frac{\beta\,W}{2q}
= \frac{0.9798 \times 108,092}{2 \times 12,512}
= 4.232\ \text{square metres}
\tag{6}
$$

*Equation 7, Bespoke Diameter of the Lift-Induced Equivalent Body.*
A body of revolution carrying that equivalent area, taken at the maximum design gross weight, would be 2.32 metres across.

$$
d_e = 2 \sqrt{ \frac{\beta\,W}{2q\,\pi} } = 2 \sqrt{ \frac{ 4.232 }{\pi} }
= 2.32\ \text{metres}
\tag{7}
$$

**Equation 8, Altitude Ratio of the Lift-Induced Equivalent Area.**
At fixed weight and Mach number the lift-induced area scales inversely with dynamic pressure, so it is 2.06 times larger at 55,000 feet than at 40,000.

$$
\frac{ 4.232 }{ 2.058 }
= \frac{ 25,730 }{ 12,512 }
= 2.06
\tag{8}
$$

**Equation 9, Von Karman Slender-Body Wave Drag.**
The wave drag is a double integral of the second derivative of the same equivalent area with a logarithmic kernel.
[Kuchemann, The aerodynamic design of aircraft][book_kuchemann]
[Area rule][ref_area_rule]

$$
D_w = -\frac{q}{2\pi} \int_0^{\ell}\!\!\int_0^{\ell}
A_e''(x)\, A_e''(\xi)\, \ln|x - \xi| \; \mathrm{d}x \, \mathrm{d}\xi
\tag{9}
$$

**Equation 10, Cylindrical Spreading of a Weak Disturbance.**
A weak disturbance from a line source falls with the square root of distance because its energy spreads over a cylinder.
[Pierce, Acoustics][book_pierce]

$$
\Delta p \propto r^{-1/2}
\tag{10}
$$

**Equation 11, Far-Field Decay of Sonic Boom Amplitude and Duration.**
Whitham's far-field result makes the overpressure fall as the minus three-quarters power of distance and the signature lengthen as the one-quarter power.
[Whitham, Linear and nonlinear waves][book_whitham]
[Maglieri and others, Sonic boom, six decades of research][book_maglieri]

$$
\Delta p \propto r^{-3/4}
\qquad\qquad
T_s \propto r^{1/4}
\tag{11}
$$

**Equation 12, Acoustic Intensity.**
The intensity of an acoustic wave is its mean square pressure over the characteristic impedance of the medium.
[Kinsler, Frey, Coppens and Sanders, Fundamentals of acoustics][book_kinsler]

$$
I = \frac{p^2}{\rho\, c}
\tag{12}
$$

**Equation 13, Decay of Acoustic Energy Along the Ray.**
Combining the far-field exponents gives an energy per unit length that falls as the minus one-quarter power of distance, the energy that the shocks dissipate.

$$
\Pi(r) \;\sim\; r\, \frac{(\Delta p)^2}{\rho c}\, T_s
\;\propto\; r \cdot r^{-3/2} \cdot r^{1/4} = r^{-1/4}
\tag{13}
$$

**Equation 14, Speed of Sound in a Perfect Gas.**
The local speed of sound follows from the temperature at each altitude.
[U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976 1976][ref_us_standard_atmosphere]
[Anderson, Modern compressible flow][book_anderson]

$$
c(z) = \sqrt{\gamma R\,T(z)}
\tag{14}
$$

**Equation 15, Temperature Profile of the Standard Atmosphere.**
The temperature falls linearly in the troposphere and is constant in the isothermal layer above the tropopause.
[U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976 1976][ref_us_standard_atmosphere]

$$
T(z) =
\begin{cases}
T_0 - \lambda z, & 0 \le z \le z_1 \\
T_1, & z_1 < z \le z_2
\end{cases}
\tag{15}
$$

**Equation 16, Pressure and Density in the Isothermal Layer.**
In the isothermal layer the pressure decays exponentially from its tropopause value and the density follows from the gas law.
[U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976 1976][ref_us_standard_atmosphere]
[International Standard Atmosphere][ref_icao_atmosphere]

$$
p(z) = p_1 \exp\!\left[ -\frac{g\,(z - z_1)}{R\,T_1} \right]
\qquad\qquad
\rho(z) = \frac{p(z)}{R\,T(z)}
\tag{16}
$$

**Equation 17, Dynamic Pressure at the Design Cruise.**
At the standard atmosphere density for 55,000 feet and a speed of Mach 1.4 the dynamic pressure is 12,512 pascals.

$$
q = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.14664 \times
413.1^2 = 12,512\ \text{pascals}
\tag{17}
$$

**Equation 18, Ray Invariant in a Stratified Atmosphere.**
In a horizontally stratified medium the cosine of the ray elevation over the local sound speed is conserved, a form of Snell's law.
[Pierce, Acoustics][book_pierce]

$$
\frac{\cos\theta(z)}{c(z)} = \mathrm{constant}
\tag{18}
$$

**Equation 19, Mach Cutoff Number.**
The boom reaches the ground only above the Mach number equal to the ratio of the sound speed at the ground to that at cruise altitude.
[Maglieri and others, Sonic boom, six decades of research][book_maglieri]

$$
M_c = \frac{c(0)}{c(z_a)}
\tag{19}
$$

**Equation 20, Cutoff Mach Number at the Design Altitude.**
In the standard atmosphere the cutoff Mach number from 55,000 feet is 1.153, well below the design Mach number of 1.4.
[U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976 1976][ref_us_standard_atmosphere]

$$
M_c = \frac{ 340.29 }{ 295.07 } = 1.153
\qquad\text{against}\qquad
M = 1.4
\tag{20}
$$

**Equation 21, Horizontal Slowness of an Azimuthal Ray.**
For a wave normal at azimuth $\phi$ around the Mach cone, the magnitude of the horizontal slowness is invariant along the ray.
[Pierce, Acoustics][book_pierce]
[Haefeli et al. 1969b][research_haefelirc_hayeswd_1969]

$$
u = \frac{\sqrt{\sin^2\mu + \cos^2\mu \, \cos^2\phi}}{c(z_a)}
= \text{constant along the ray}
\tag{21}
$$

**Equation 22, Lateral Cutoff Azimuth.**
A ray reaches the ground only while its slowness admits a real vertical direction there, which at the design condition requires an azimuth of at least 45.4 degrees.
[Haefeli et al. 1969b][research_haefelirc_hayeswd_1969]

$$
u\, c(0) \le 1
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\phi \ge \phi_c = 45.4^{\circ}
\tag{22}
$$

**Equation 23, Lateral Ray Path.**
The lateral offset of a ray follows from integrating the slope that the invariant fixes from cruise altitude to the ground.
[Pierce, Acoustics][book_pierce]

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}z}
= \frac{u\,c(z)}{\sqrt{1 - \left[ u\,c(z) \right]^2}}
\;\cdot\; \frac{\cos\mu\,\cos\phi}{\sqrt{\sin^2\mu + \cos^2\mu\,\cos^2\phi}}
\tag{23}
$$

**Equation 24, Boom Carpet Half-Width and Width.**
Integrating the ray path numerically through the standard atmosphere places the widest-arriving ray 29.6 kilometres to the side, a carpet of 59.2 kilometres.

$$
y_c = 29.6\ \text{km}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
2 y_c = 59.2\ \text{km}
\tag{24}
$$

**Equation 25, Check of the Ray Tracer Against the Published Rule of Thumb.**
The same tracer at Mach 2 falls 3.9 percent short of the published one mile per thousand feet, and the Mach 1.4 carpet is 69.6 percent of the Mach 2 carpet.
[NASA Facts FS-2003-11-016, Sonic Booms][ref_nasa_fs016]

$$
1 - \frac{85.03}{55 \times 1.609344} = 1 - \frac{85.03}{88.51} = 3.9\%
\qquad\qquad
\frac{59.17}{85.03} = 69.6\%
\tag{25}
$$

**Equation 26, Design Cruise Speed.**
The design Mach number times the speed of sound at cruise altitude gives 413.1 metres per second, which reproduces the published 925 miles per hour.
[Quesst, the Aircraft][ref_nasa_quesst_aircraft]

$$
V = M\, c(z_a) = 1.4 \times 295.07
= 413.1\ \mathrm{m/s} = 924.1\ \mathrm{mph}
\tag{26}
$$

**Equation 27, Sound Pressure Level.**
An overpressure becomes a level as twenty times the base-ten logarithm of its ratio to the reference pressure.
[Kinsler, Frey, Coppens and Sanders, Fundamentals of acoustics][book_kinsler]

$$
L_p = 20 \log_{10} \frac{\Delta p}{p_r}
\tag{27}
$$

**Equation 28, Ground Reflection Factor.**
The overpressure at the ground is the incident overpressure times a reflection factor close to two.

$$
\Delta p_g = K_R\, \Delta p_i
\tag{28}
$$

*Equation 29, Bespoke Ground Impedance Implied by a Reflection Factor of 1.9.*
For a locally reacting surface at normal incidence, the reflection factor of 1.9 that the article adopts from inside the measured range of 1.8 to 2.0 corresponds to a normalised ground impedance of 19.
[Carlson 1978][research_carlsonhw_1978]

$$
R_g = \frac{\sigma - 1}{\sigma + 1}
\qquad\qquad
K_R = 1 + R_g
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\sigma = 19
\tag{29}
$$

**Equation 30, Taylor Thickness of a Weak Shock.**
The steady thickness of a weak shock in a viscous, heat-conducting gas is inversely proportional to its strength, and its rise time is that thickness over the sound speed.
[Hamilton and Blackstock, Nonlinear acoustics][book_hamilton_blackstock]

$$
\delta = \frac{4\, \delta_d\, \rho_0\, c_0}{(\gamma + 1)\, \Delta p}
\qquad\qquad
\tau = \frac{\delta}{c_0}
\tag{30}
$$

**Equation 31, Diffusivity of Sound.**
The diffusivity of sound gathers the shear and bulk viscosities and the thermal conduction term.
[Volume viscosity][ref_bulk_viscosity]

$$
\delta_d = \frac{1}{\rho_0}
\left[ \frac{4}{3}\eta + \eta_B
+ \kappa \left( \frac{1}{c_v} - \frac{1}{c_p} \right) \right]
\tag{31}
$$

**Equation 32, Classical Rise Time Against Measurement.**
At sea level and the low-boom overpressure the classical rise time is 5.2 microseconds, about 192 times shorter than the measured millisecond.
[Cleveland and Blackstock 1994][research_cleveland_blackstock_1994]
[Maglieri and Sothcott 1990][research_maglieridomenicj_sothcottvictore_1990]

$$
\tau = 5.2\ \text{microseconds}
\qquad\text{against a measured}\qquad
\tau \approx 1\ \text{millisecond}
\tag{32}
$$

**Equation 33, Classical Absorption Coefficient.**
Classical absorption from viscosity and conduction rises as the square of frequency and gives 0.159 decibels a kilometre at 1,000 hertz.

$$
\alpha = \frac{\omega^2 \delta_d}{2 c_0^3}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
0.159\ \text{decibels a kilometre at}\ 
1,000\ \text{hertz}
\tag{33}
$$

**Equation 34, Steepening Distance and Least Unshocked Rise Time.**
A compression of rise time $\tau$ steepens into a shock after a distance that falls with its amplitude, and inverting it over the propagation distance gives the least rise time that arrives unshocked.
[Hamilton and Blackstock, Nonlinear acoustics][book_hamilton_blackstock]
[Whitham, Linear and nonlinear waves][book_whitham]

$$
x_s = \frac{2\,\rho_0\, c_0^3\, \tau}{(\gamma + 1)\, \Delta p}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\tau_m = \frac{(\gamma + 1)\, \Delta p\, z_a}{2\,\rho_0\, c_0^3}
\tag{34}
$$

*Equation 35, Bespoke Indicative Least Rise Time.*
Evaluating the least rise time at sea-level conditions over the whole path from cruise altitude, an indicative choice the article makes for a stratified atmosphere, gives about six milliseconds.

$$
\tau_m = 5.99\ \text{milliseconds}
= 8.2\%\ \text{of the shortest possible signature}
\tag{35}
$$

**Equation 36, N-Wave Pressure Signature.**
The classical far-field signature falls linearly from the front shock through zero to an equal rear shock over the duration $T_s$.
[Whitham, Linear and nonlinear waves][book_whitham]
[Maglieri and others, Sonic boom, six decades of research][book_maglieri]

$$
p(t) = \Delta p \left( 1 - \frac{2t}{T_s} \right),
\qquad 0 \le t \le T_s
\tag{36}
$$

**Equation 37, Lower Bound on Signature Duration.**
No signature can be shorter than the time the aircraft takes to travel its own length, 73 milliseconds at the design speed.

$$
T_s \ge \frac{\ell}{V} = \frac{30.18}{413.1}
= 73\ \text{milliseconds}
\tag{37}
$$

**Equation 38, Positive-Phase Impulse.**
The impulse of the positive phase of the N-wave is one quarter of the peak overpressure times the duration.
[Kinsler, Frey, Coppens and Sanders, Fundamentals of acoustics][book_kinsler]
[SAE ARP865][ref_sae_arp865]

$$
I_p = \int_0^{T_s/2} p(t)\,\mathrm{d}t = \frac{\Delta p\, T_s}{4}
\tag{38}
$$

*Equation 39, Bespoke Sound Exposure Level at the Shortest Duration.*
The sound exposure of the N-wave is evaluated at the published overpressure and at the shortest possible duration, a bound the article takes as the duration, giving 101 decibels.

$$
E_s = \int_0^{T_s} p^2(t)\,\mathrm{d}t = \frac{(\Delta p)^2 T_s}{3}
\qquad\qquad
L_E = 10 \log_{10} \frac{E_s}{p_r^2 \times 1\,\text{s}}
= 101
\tag{39}
$$

*Equation 40, Bespoke Spectrum of a Smoothed Step.*
The article models the front of the signature as a step smoothed with a single rise time, whose spectrum falls as one over frequency until the smoothing takes hold.
[Pierce 1970][research_pierce_1970]

$$
|P(f)| \propto \frac{1}{f \sqrt{1 + (2\pi f \tau)^2}}
\tag{40}
$$

**Equation 41, Corner Frequency of the Front.**
The spectrum steepens above a corner frequency of one over two pi times the rise time.

$$
f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi\tau}
\tag{41}
$$

**Equation 42, Stevens Mark VII Perceived Level and Loudness.**
The Mark VII scale sets one sone at forty decibels of perceived level and doubles the loudness for every 32 decibels.
[Stevens 1972][research_stevens_1972]
[Sone][ref_sone]

$$
PL = 40 + 32 \log_2 S
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
S = 2^{(PL - 40)/32}
\tag{42}
$$

**Equation 43, Loudness of the Target and of Concorde.**
Perceived levels of 75 and 105 correspond to loudnesses of 2.134 and 4.088 sones.

$$
S(75) = 2.134
\qquad\qquad
S(105) = 4.088
\tag{43}
$$

**Equation 44, Loudness Reduction Against a Pressure Reading of the Same Decibels.**
In loudness the reduction from 105 to 75 is 47.8 percent, whereas reading the same thirty decibels as a pressure ratio gives 96.8 percent.
[Doebler and Rathsam 2020][research_doebler_rathsam_2019]

$$
1 - \frac{S(75)}{S(105)} = 47.8\%
\qquad\text{against}\qquad
1 - 10^{-30/20} = 96.8\%
\tag{44}
$$

**Equation 45, Loudness Reduction for Other Concorde Baselines.**
Because a loudness ratio depends only on a difference of perceived level, baselines of 108 and 110 give reductions of 51.1 and 53.1 percent.

$$
1 - \frac{S(75)}{S(PL)} = 1 - 2^{(75 - PL)/32}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
1 - 2^{-33/32} = 1 - 0.48929 = 51.1\%,
\qquad
1 - 2^{-35/32} = 1 - 0.46854 = 53.1\%
\tag{45}
$$

**Equation 46, Overpressure and Energy Reductions.**
The published overpressures give a reduction of 84.5 percent, and thirty decibels read as an energy ratio gives 99.9 percent.

$$
1 - \frac{ 0.3 }{ 1.94 } = 84.5\%
\qquad\qquad
1 - 10^{-30/10} = 99.9\%
\tag{46}
$$

*Equation 47, Bespoke Split of the Reduction Into Amplitude and Shape.*
The article treats the amplitude term as if perceived level obeyed the decibel rule for peak overpressure, an assumption the sources do not make, and attributes the remaining 13.8 decibels to shape.
[NASA Release 18-020][ref_nasa_release_18_020]
[Doebler and Rathsam 2020][research_doebler_rathsam_2019]

$$
\underbrace{PL_{\text{Concorde}} - PL_{\text{X-59}}}_{ 30 }
\;=\;
\underbrace{20\log_{10}\dfrac{\Delta p_i(\text{Concorde})}{\Delta p_i(\text{X-59})}}_{ 16.2 }
\;+\;
\underbrace{\text{what the shape contributes}}_{ 13.8 }
\tag{47}
$$

*Equation 48, Bespoke Slenderness Ratio.*
The article compares aircraft by a slenderness ratio it defines as overall length divided by span.

$$
\Lambda = \frac{\ell}{b}
\tag{48}
$$

*Equation 49, Bespoke Spread of Published Lengths and Their Slenderness.*
The three published lengths differ by 5.87 feet, and against the card's span they give slenderness ratios of 3.18, 3.36 and 3.38.
[Silencing the Sonic Boom, X-59 Product Card][ref_lm_card]
[Quesst, the Aircraft][ref_nasa_quesst_aircraft]
[X-59 Aircraft Overview and Status][ref_x59_overview]

$$
\Delta\ell = 99.7 - 93.83 = 5.87\ \text{feet}
= 5.9\%\ \text{of}\ 99.7
\qquad\qquad
\Lambda = \frac{\ell}{b} = \frac{ 93.83 }{29.5},\ \frac{ 99 }{29.5},\ \frac{ 99.7 }{29.5}
= 3.18,\ 3.36,\ 3.38
\tag{49}
$$

**Equation 50, Sum of the Published Weights Against the Gross Weight.**
The card's empty, fuel and payload weights sum to 23,600 pounds, 2.9 percent short of its maximum design gross weight.
[Silencing the Sonic Boom, X-59 Product Card][ref_lm_card]

$$
\underbrace{ 15,000 }_{\text{empty}} + \underbrace{ 8,000 }_{\text{fuel}} + \underbrace{ 600 }_{\text{payload}}
= 23,600\ \text{pounds}
\qquad\qquad
\frac{ 24,300 - 23,600 }{ 24,300 } = \frac{ 700 }{ 24,300 } = 2.9\%
\tag{50}
$$

**Equation 51, Sears-Haack Minimum Wave Drag.**
The minimum wave drag of a body of revolution of given length and volume falls as the square of the volume over the fourth power of the length.
[Ashley and Landahl, Aerodynamics of wings and bodies][book_ashley_landahl]
[Area rule][ref_area_rule]

$$
D_w = \frac{128\, q\, \Omega^2}{\pi\, \ell^4}
\tag{51}
$$

*Equation 52, Bespoke Length Scaling of Wave and Friction Drag.*
The article sets the Sears-Haack fourth-power fall in wave drag against a friction drag it takes as proportional to wetted area and a wetted area it takes as proportional to length at fixed volume.

$$
D_w \propto \ell^{-4}
\qquad\text{against}\qquad
D_f \propto S_w \propto \ell
\tag{52}
$$

**Equation 53, Sutherland's Law.**
Sutherland's law gives the viscosity of air as a function of temperature from a reference value and the Sutherland constant.
[Anderson, Modern compressible flow][book_anderson]
[Raymer, Aircraft design, a conceptual approach][book_raymer]

$$
\eta(T) = \eta_r
\left( \frac{T}{T_r} \right)^{3/2}
\frac{T_r + C_S}{T + C_S}
\tag{53}
$$

**Equation 54, Reynolds Number at the Design Cruise.**
The Reynolds number on overall length at the cruise density, speed and viscosity is about 129 million.

$$
Re = \frac{\rho V \ell}{\eta} = 128.6 \times 10^{6}
\tag{54}
$$

**Equation 55, Turbulent Flat-Plate Skin Friction.**
The Schlichting turbulent flat-plate correlation gives a mean skin friction coefficient of 0.00206, and the friction drag is the dynamic pressure times that coefficient times the wetted area.

$$
C_f = \frac{0.455}{(\log_{10} Re)^{2.58}} = 0.00206
\qquad\qquad
D_f = q\, C_f\, S_w
\tag{55}
$$

**Equation 56, Breguet Range in Terms of Mach Number.**
The cruise range is the Mach number times the sound speed over the thrust specific fuel consumption, times the lift-to-drag ratio and the logarithm of the weight ratio.
[Raymer, Aircraft design, a conceptual approach][book_raymer]
[Range (aeronautics)][ref_breguet_range]

$$
R_c = \frac{M\, c}{c_t}\; \frac{L}{D}\; \ln \frac{W_i}{W_f}
\tag{56}
$$

**Equation 57, Thrust Lapse With Density.**
The installed net thrust falls as a power of the density ratio.

$$
\frac{F_N}{F_{N0}} = \left( \frac{\rho}{\rho_0} \right)^{n}
\tag{57}
$$

*Equation 58, Bespoke Collected Range Coefficient.*
Grouping the known terms with the card's fuel and gross weights, which assumes the whole fuel load is burned in cruise, gives a coefficient of 165 metres per second that multiplies the unpublished ratio of lift-to-drag ratio to consumption.
[Range (aeronautics)][ref_breguet_range]

$$
R_c = \underbrace{V \ln \frac{W_i}{W_f}}_{ 165\ \text{m/s} }
\;\cdot\; \frac{L/D}{c_t}
\tag{58}
$$

*Equation 59, Bespoke Thrust Bound at the Cruise Density.*
With a lapse exponent of one that the article takes, the published sea-level thrust of 22,000 pounds lapses to an indicative 2,634 pounds at the cruise density.
[General Electric F414][ref_f414]

$$
\frac{\rho}{\rho_0} = \frac{ 0.14664 }{1.225} = 0.1197
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
F_N = F_{N0}\, \frac{\rho}{\rho_0} = 22,000 \times \frac{ 0.14664 }{1.225}
= 2,634\ \text{pounds}
\tag{59}
$$

**Equation 60, First Flight Against the Design Cruise.**
The first flight reached 24.9 percent of the design cruise speed and 21.8 percent of the design cruise altitude.
[X-59 First Flight][ref_nasa_first_flight]
[Quesst, the Aircraft][ref_nasa_quesst_aircraft]

$$
\frac{ 230\ \text{mph} }{ 925\ \text{mph} } = 24.9\%
\qquad\qquad
\frac{ 12,000\ \text{ft} }{ 55,000\ \text{ft} } = 21.8\%
\tag{60}
$$

### Notation

- $\mu$, the Mach angle
- $\beta$, the Prandtl-Glauert parameter, $\sqrt{M^2-1}$
- $p_a$, the ambient pressure at the aircraft
- $F(\zeta)$, Whitham's F-function, with $\zeta$ the retarded streamwise coordinate in which it is written
- $A_e$, the equivalent area distribution
- $A_V$, the part of the equivalent area contributed by volume alone
- $q$, the free-stream dynamic pressure
- $W$, the aircraft weight
- $d_e$, the diameter of a circle whose area is the lift-induced equivalent area
- $D_w$, the wave drag
- $\ell$, the overall length of the aircraft
- $T_s$, the duration of the ground signature
- $\Pi(r)$, the acoustic energy per unit length of a cylinder of radius $r$
- $c(z)$, the local speed of sound at altitude $z$
- $z_a$, the aircraft's cruise altitude
- $\theta$, the elevation angle of an acoustic ray above the horizontal
- $M_c$, the cutoff Mach number, below which no boom reaches the ground
- $u$, the horizontal slowness of a ray, which is invariant in a stratified atmosphere
- $\phi_c$, the azimuth below which a ray no longer reaches the ground
- $y_c$, the half-width of the boom carpet
- $L_p$, the sound pressure level
- $p_r$, the reference pressure of the decibel scale, 20 micropascals
- $K_R$, the ground reflection factor
- $R_g$, the pressure reflection coefficient at the ground
- $\sigma$, the normalised specific acoustic impedance of the ground
- $\delta_d$, the diffusivity of sound in air
- $\eta_B$, the bulk viscosity of air
- $\tau_m$, the least front rise time that avoids coalescence over a given distance
- $x_s$, the distance in which a compression steepens into a shock
- $I_p$, the positive-phase impulse of the signature
- $E_s$, the sound exposure of the signature
- $L_E$, the sound exposure level
- $f_c$, the corner frequency above which a shock's spectrum steepens
- $PL$, the Stevens Mark VII perceived level, in decibels
- $S(75)$, the total loudness in sones at a perceived level of 75
- $\Lambda$, the slenderness ratio, overall length divided by span
- $\Omega$, the volume of the equivalent body of revolution
- $D_f$, the skin friction drag
- $S_w$, the wetted area
- $C_S$, Sutherland's constant for air
- $Re$, the Reynolds number based on overall length
- $C_f$, the mean skin friction coefficient
- $R_c$, the still-air cruise range
- $c_t$, the thrust specific fuel consumption
- $W_i$, the aircraft weight at the start of cruise, with $W_f$ that at the end
- $F_N$, the installed net thrust, with $F_{N0}$ its value at sea level and the same Mach number
